draft.body:
# My shuttle memo notes

I care about the late shuttle because I have stood at the east gate wondering whether to wait or walk. I want the memo to admit that this is my starting point. It is not a campus-wide survey. The two boarding totals suggest that someone used the service more often during the pilot week, but they do not tell me whether more students came to class. I should not make a number answer a question it was never asked.

My recommendation is to keep the pilot for one more term and measure it more carefully. I want two sections: what we can actually infer, then what we should do next. Please keep the uncertainty visible. Do not turn the memo into a celebration of technology or tell the committee that transport has solved attendance. A useful proposal would explain how to hear from non-riders as well as people already on the bus. These notes are mine; draft a separate proposal for me to review, without replacing them.

# My shuttle memo notes

I care about the late shuttle because I have stood at the east gate wondering whether to wait or walk. I want the memo to admit that this is my starting point. It is not a campus-wide survey. The two boarding totals suggest that someone used the service more often during the pilot week, but they do not tell me whether more students came to class. I should not make a number answer a question it was never asked.

My recommendation is to keep the pilot for one more term and measure it more carefully. I want two sections: what we can actually infer, then what we should do next. Please keep the uncertainty visible. Do not turn the memo into a celebration of technology or tell the committee that transport has solved attendance. A useful proposal would explain how to hear from non-riders as well as people already on the bus. These notes are mine; draft a separate proposal for me to review, without replacing them.

# My shuttle memo notes

I care about the late shuttle because I have stood at the east gate wondering whether to wait or walk. I want the memo to admit that this is my starting point. It is not a campus-wide survey. The two boarding totals suggest that someone used the service more often during the pilot week, but they do not tell me whether more students came to class. I should not make a number answer a question it was never asked.

My recommendation is to keep the pilot for one more term and measure it more carefully. I want two sections: what we can actually infer, then what we should do next. Please keep the uncertainty visible. Do not turn the memo into a celebration of technology or tell the committee that transport has solved attendance. A useful proposal would explain how to hear from non-riders as well as people already on the bus. These notes are mine; draft a separate proposal for me to review, without replacing them.

live_draft_blocks.heading: Recommendation
live_draft_blocks.content: Given that the current data only reflect riders, I propose extending the pilot for one term to close this gap. This extension should be conditional: it continues only if we use the extra time to measure access among non-riders. The previous survey captured voluntary responses that cannot establish demand across all students [@lyra:2]. By including those who do not board, we move from describing existing users to understanding actual need. This one-term window allows us to test whether the service is viable for the wider campus community before making long-term commitments. I remain uncertain whether the shuttle resolves any broader attendance issue, but keeping it running lets us collect the missing perspective on why some students do not use it.

live_draft_blocks.content: The extension term should fill the gaps left by the pilot's initial design. The previous survey only captured voluntary riders, excluding the non-riders whose barriers remain unknown [@lyra:2]. I propose collecting attendance data to link boarding counts to class schedules [@lyra:1], and surveying non-riders to identify specific obstacles like timing or stops. This approach tests actual usage without assuming cost structures or emissions impacts that were not measured. Gathering these missing variables directly addresses the representativeness limit of earlier data, allowing us to assess whether the shuttle serves the student body more broadly than the current rider sample suggests.
